This signpost carries the laws of Cormyr.

1. All those entering Cormyr must register with the officials.
2. Please exchange all foreign currency to Cormyrian golden lions or Trade Bars. Foreign currency is not accepted within Cormyr.
3. No Adventuring permitted without an Adventurer's Charter, obtainable at the Crown Office.
4. All weapons must be peace-bonded, except those that can prove gainful employment that requires the use of un-bonded weapons.
5. Harming cats is forbidden.
6. Respect to the nobility is required in Cormyr.
7. The Purple Dragons have the right to search you on request.
8. Hunting on private land is forbidden.

The founding of the Kingdom of Cormyr and the identity of the first King in Suzail is debated among scholars.  One minor school of thought considers a farmer known only as  "Mondar" the first leader of the settlement of Suzail, and, accordingly, the true "first king". 

A more popular theory among historians in the Royal Court holds that Ondeth Obarskyr was, in fact, the first king of Cormyr.  There is no dispute that Ondeth Obarskyr was, in his day, the true leader of his people; however, Ondeth did not style himself as a king. Indeed, Ondeth refused the title of king and any crown that was purported to be granted or affirmed by the elves. Ondeth is famed among his descendants for supposedly vowing loudly "no title is preferable to one tainted by a false duty of fealty to any elven sovereign". 

Whatever the case, the court historians generally agree that about 1,350 years ago in The Year of Opening Doors (26 DR)  Faerlthann Obarskyr, son of Ondeth met with the elven King Iliphar Nelnueve, Lord of the Scepters and his court near the ruined site of a famous goblin raid.  There, Iliphar gave to Faerlthann Obarskyr the circlet of Cormanthor from his own brow and the first knights of Cormyr knelt to swear fealty to House Obarskyr.
House Obarskyr - The Royal Lineage of Cormyr

Legend recalls that the Kingdom of Cormyr was in ancient days a heavily forested land inundated by dozens of great dragons of many colors.  Then, as now, the forests of Cormyr were characterized by rich game and served as prime hunting grounds for the great beasts of the Dragon Reach.

While the dragons of Cormyr were many and large, the "Land of the Purple Dragon" takes its name from the greatest of the dragons who dwelled in it, Thauglorimorgorus, also called "Thauglor the Mighty" and "Thauglor the Black Doom".

Thauglor was not a "purple" dragon at all, but rather a great black dragon who was so old that his scales had changed color from dark ebony to violet.  In the light, the great wyrm's scales were said to have sparkled a deep, rich purple.

Since those days of the epic battles between Thauglor the Mighty and the great elven king who defeated the dragon in a duel, the sages say the Land of the Purple Dragon has always belonged to Thauglor the Mighty.

There have been many threats to the Kingdom of Cormyr over the centuries, but no peril has ever been as great as that faced by King Galaghard III and High Wizard Thanderahast in the Year of the Thirsty Sword. 

In that year a great host of goblins, orcs, ogres, and human mercenaries had allied itself with a vast army of undead under the control of a powerful Order of Necromancers from the East, known as the Witch Lords. The Witch Lords' purpose was plain - they meant to conquer and enslave Cormyr.  Master tacticians as well as fell sorcerers, the Witch Lords' lieutenants flew on great shrieking bats, while the most powerful of the great necromancers commanded the battlefield astride large wyverns of the deep forest. Armored in fear as well as steel, the Witch Lords were said to inspire dread in any mortal who gazed upon them.
 
Despite the whole of the marshalled knights of the kingdom and the disciplined Purple Dragons, Cormyr nearly fell to the Witch Lords in a great battle between what was then the border between the Hullack Forest and the Vast Swamp.  But as the necromancers' army was set to sweep aside the left flank of the defenders and encircle the King's remaining knights, an elven army emerged out of the woods and onto the battlefield.

Taking the Witch Lords by surprise, the army of the elves shattered the orc lines. At a stroke, the mortal soldiers of the Witch Lords were broken and fled the field. With grim determination, the remaining undead host of the Witch Lords was put to the sword by the combined might of Cormyr and the elven King, Othorion Keove.  And so it was that the Kingdom of Cormyr was preserved.

Master tacticians as well as fell sorcerers, the Witch Lords' lieutenants flew on great shrieking bats, while the most powerful of the great necromancers commanded the battlefield astride large wyverns of the deep forest. Armored in fear as well as steel, the Witch Lords were said to inspire dread in any mortal who gazed upon them.
 
Despite the whole of the marshalled knights of the kingdom and the disciplined Purple Dragons, Cormyr nearly fell to the Witch Lords in a great battle between what was then the border between the Hullack Forest and the Vast Swamp.  But as the necromancers' army was set to sweep aside the left flank of the defenders and encircle the King's remaining knights, an elven army emerged out of the woods and onto the battlefield.

Taking the Witch Lords by surprise, the army of the elves shattered the orc lines. At a stroke, the mortal soldiers of the Witch Lords were broken and fled the field. With grim determination, the remaining undead host of the Witch Lords was put to the sword by the combined might of Cormyr and the elven King, Othorion Keove.  And so it was that the Kingdom of Cormyr was preserved.

Jousting is an ancient tradition in Cormyr and many other lands. In times of peace, it has always been difficult for aspiring knights and lords to find a way to prove their prowess to their peers or their king. Jousting became a method for one knight to prove his superiority over another. Soon such contests became more formal, and even the right to hold a tournament itself became a source of influence. Jousting is now a very popular way to gain fame, influence or even power. 

The aim in a joust is to unseat your opponent from his or her horse, by means of a specially designed jousting lance. These lances are specially designed to break on impact in order to lessen the chance of injuries, but a perfect blow is still more likely to unseat an opponent than leave them in the saddle.

Arcane language has sprung up around jousting, and it is now commonplace to refer to strikes by the area of the shield they aim for:

Pale: the central line running vertically down the shield
Fess: The central line running horizontally across the shield
Chief: The top third of the shield
Base: The bottom third of the shield
Sinister: The left side of the shield
Dexter: The right side of the shield

Scoring
Jousting matches are split into bouts, or 'tilts'. In each bout the two opponents ride at each other. The scoring for a bout is as follows:

Opponent unseated - 3 points
Opponent's helm struck - 2 points
Competitor's own lance breaks - 1 point

When either competitor has reached 3 points, they have won the match. In the case of a tie, the bouts continue until one or other jouster has more points. Typically points are denoted using flags. Most tournament masters use only three flags for each competitor. A fourth flag is only used to denote a winner in the case of a tie-break situation.

Aggressive Strikes
The aggressive strikes in jousting are considered to be Pale Chief, Pale Fess and Helm. Typically these blows are more likely to score points, though the downside of using these strikes is that they limit the knight's seating, in turn making them more vulnerable.

Defensive Strikes
